prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I swallowed the sweet thing in a dream. I woke up heavy. I said, what’s the matter with you. I said, stop seeing what’s the matter with me. I ran to/from only moving one frantic eye. Something snitched. Then back to the argument. It is more acceptable to steal from the ether. When you said, we take matters into our own hands. I didn’t start the day with a ritual. Again. Twenty days and counting! I said, I was supposed to address my wrongs to you. The sweetgrass still in its plastic. Keep it there for its poetry? Then the driftwood resting on my father’s ashes. Well, you said, ecstasy from a fluted throat. Ha. As if there were presence enough in me to notice, before this. I said, I’m less angry now that you don’t exist. Then the aha moment announced. Whistling nothing like wind through fistulae. That happens here. Left to my own devices, I said. As if language were a refuge. As though the sound of walls.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Something, Then, When

outputs.L1:
Here are two polished versions tailored to different literary tones. Both preserve every detail, image, and meaning of your original text while elevating the cadence, vocabulary, and phrasing.

### Option 1: Literary & Evocative (Recommended)
*This version refines the stream-of-consciousness rhythm into high-register poetic prose, accentuating its dramatic depth and lyricism.*

> "In a dream, I swallowed something sweet, yet I awoke laden with weight. *'What is wrong with you?'* I asked. *'Stop searching for what is wrong with me,'* I countered. I fled between retreat and advance, moving with only a single, frantic eye. Something betrayed the secret, and we returned to the argument. It seems far more permissible to steal from the ether—especially when you declared that we ought to take matters into our own hands. 
> 
> Once again, I failed to begin the day with ritual. Twenty days now, and counting. I told you I was meant to address my transgressions to you. The sweetgrass remains encased in plastic—shall I preserve it merely for the poetry of it? Beside it, driftwood rests upon my father’s ashes. *'Ecstasy from a fluted throat,'* you once remarked. Ha. As if I possessed enough presence to notice such things before this. 
> 
> *'I am less angry now that you no longer exist,'* I said. Then came the epiphany, announcing itself like the hollow whistle of wind passing through a fistula. Such things happen here. *'Left to my own devices,'* I murmured—as though language could offer sanctuary; as though the sound of walls could ever suffice."

---

### Option 2: Smooth & Elegant Prose
*This version seamlessly blends the fragments into a continuous, reflective narrative while retaining the original enigmatic mood.*

> "I swallowed a sweet thing in my sleep and awoke with a profound heaviness. I asked myself what was wrong, then demanded that I stop probing for flaws. I ran—neither fully toward nor away—guided by a single, frantic eye. A betrayal occurred, drawing us right back into the dispute. It feels far more acceptable to pull answers from the ether, particularly after you insisted we take matters into our own hands. 
> 
> Another day has passed without a morning ritual—twenty days and counting. I admitted that I was supposed to bring my grievances to you. The sweetgrass is still wrapped in its plastic; do I leave it there simply to preserve the aesthetic? Meanwhile, a piece of driftwood rests over my father’s ashes. You spoke once of 'ecstasy from a fluted throat,' but I lacked the presence of mind to appreciate it until now. 
> 
> I told you I feel less anger now that you do not exist. Then, an epiphany announced itself—a sound resembling nothing so much as wind whistling through a fistula. That is simply how things occur here. 'Left to my own devices,' I said, pretending language were a true refuge, as if the mere sound of walls could hold."
outputs.L2:
During a sleep state, I ingested something sugary, causing me to awaken with a feeling of deep lethargy. A back-and-forth ensued where I asked what was wrong, followed by my insistence that my flaws no longer be scrutinized. I moved around erratically, my attention focused through a single wildly darting eye, just as an act of betrayal occurred, plunging me right back into our debate. 

It is considered far more permissible to siphon from the intangible void, despite your statement that we must take control of our own circumstances. Once again, I failed to start my morning with my usual ceremonial habit—a streak that has now reached twenty consecutive days. I noted that I was obligated to admit my misdeeds to you. Meanwhile, the bundle of sweetgrass remains sealed inside its synthetic wrapping; perhaps it stays unsealed for its symbolic value? Next to it, a piece of sea-worn timber sits atop the container holding my late father’s remains. 

You had previously spoken of bliss emanating from a grooved, tubular channel—a claim I greet with irony, given that I lacked the conscious awareness to register any of this prior to this moment. I stated that your lack of existence has actually diminished my resentment. Then, a sudden realization made itself known, creating a sound unlike a draft passing through abnormal bodily openings, which is a common occurrence in this environment. 

Abandoned to my own independence, I reflected on the naive assumption that vocabulary could serve as a sanctuary, or that any comfort could be found in the reverberations of enclosing barriers.
outputs.L3:
I awoke this morning under the suffocating weight of a dream I could not quite recall, its heavy residue clinging to my chest like damp wool. Before my eyes had even fully opened, the familiar internal court convened behind my eyelids. I found myself instinctively mounting a defensive argument, trying to shield myself from the sharp, relentless edge of my own self-scrutiny. It is an exhausting way to cross the threshold into consciousness, bracing for an interrogation from one's own mind.

This internal friction, I realize, is the result of a deeper drift. For twenty consecutive days, I have quietly abandoned the small, daily rituals that once kept me anchored to the world. On the shelf, a braid of sweetgrass sits suffocating in its original cellophane packaging—bought with the intention of cleansing my space, now left completely untouched. It remains there as a symbolic monument to my inertia, a quiet reminder of intentions that never materialized into action. 

In the stillness of this retreat, however, I have discovered that my long-held anger has begun to cool. It has not dissolved into forgiveness or understanding, but rather diminished into a hollow silence. The fierce arguments I carried in my head have lost their momentum for a simple, devastating reason: the person to whom all my grievances were addressed no longer exists. Without an adversary to receive my fury, the rage simply evaporates, leaving behind a strange, disorienting quiet.

Grief has a way of solidifying into physical forms. Nearby, a piece of gnarled driftwood rests directly atop the box containing my father’s ashes. The wood—heavier than it looks, smoothed by the slow violence of the tide—feels like an anchor holding down the dead. Staring at it, the underlying reality of mortality feels inescapable. The driftwood and the ashes speak the same silent language of erosion, reminding me of how time slowly strips away everything we once considered permanent.

Now, stripped of my rituals and my anger, I am left entirely alone with my thoughts in the quiet room. I turn to words, as I so often do, trying to weave these feelings into something coherent. Yet, an uneasy question lingers: Can language truly function as a genuine refuge from reality? Or are these words merely a delicate, desperate architecture constructed to distract me from the cold, unyielding facts of loss, time, and my own isolation?
outputs.L4:
The salt has dried in the small copper dish on the windowsill, leaving behind a crust of white residue like an eye that refuses to close. Next to it, the half-burned stick of incense sits cold, its tip long buried in its own gray powder. For months, these gestures of remembrance—the unlit candles, the small dishes of water, the dry marigolds crumbling into dust—were meant to be a bridge, or perhaps a sanctuary. Instead, they have become monuments to my own cowardice. I left the shrine to rot because I could not bear to ask who it was truly for: the one who vanished, or the guilt that stayed behind?

In the corners of this room, memory bends and fractures. I pick up a rusted key that unlocks a door we no longer own, running my thumb over its notched spine until the skin turns red. On the table lies a pocket watch with a cracked glass face, its hands frozen at three minutes past midnight—a perpetual, suspended moment of rupture. I talk to these relics as if they were witnesses in a trial where I am both the accused and the judge. Was it my silence that drove you into the dark, or was it the quiet violence of my expectations? The guilt coils around my ribs, tight and suffocating, feeding an anger that has burned so long it feels like an organ I cannot live without. I have carried our unfinished arguments like stones in my mouth, rehearsing bitter retorts to a ghost that never answers.

But tonight, the fever of the monologue breaks. The air grows unnaturally still, stripping away the poetic theater of my mourning. 

I look toward the empty chair by the doorway, waiting for the familiar weight of your absence to press against my chest, but for the first time, nothing presses back. I have spent years raging against a specter, convincing myself that your ghost was haunting these halls, demanding restitution. The surreal truth, dropping like lead into the silence, is far simpler and far more devastating: you are not here. You are not floating in the ether, nursing old wounds, nor are you silently judging my failure to keep the incense lit. You simply cease to be in this space. The anger I held so fiercely requires an antagonist, but there is no one on the other side of the rope. Pulling against a void only throws the climber to the ground. 

As the myth of your lingering presence dissolves, the heat of my fury cools into a vast, quiet clarity. The guilt does not disappear, but it loses its sharp edge; it becomes merely an artifact of a past that no longer commands the present. 

I turn away from the neglected altar and step toward the desk. The relics remain just things—metal, glass, dried petals—devoid of power. I pick up a pen, feeling the solid, unyielding weight of it between my fingers. If no spirit is coming to grant absolution, then I must construct my own. Language becomes my sole architecture, the only clean room left in a house of cluttered regrets. Line by line, I begin to name the grief without gilding it, spelling out the pain in precise, sober syntax. In the rhythm of my own voice returning to me, I find the true sanctuary. I am not saved by a gesture to the dead, but by the quiet, self-reliant act of writing myself back into the living.
outputs.L5:
There is a quiet art to waiting. Most days pass in a steady, predictable rhythm, yet beneath the surface, we are almost always holding our breath for **something**—a spark of inspiration, a shift in the tide, or a long-awaited truth to reveal itself. It is an instinctual feeling that sits just beyond the horizon of our awareness, subtle yet persistent.

**When** that moment finally arrives, it rarely announces itself with fanfare. It comes in the soft turn of a key, the sudden clearing of a stormy sky, or a single choice made in the quiet of a morning. **When** you least expect it, the familiar landscape fractures to make room for a new perspective. 

And **then**, everything begins to move. The hesitation that once held you back evaporates, replaced by a momentum that reorders the world around you. **Then**, the past folds neatly into memory, and the path forward unfolds with sudden, beautiful clarity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about grief and fragmented memory. Make the tone surreal, dreamlike, and melancholic, using disjointed sentences and internal dialogue.
counterfactuals.output:
The room is three inches narrower than it was yesterday. The linoleum buckles—no, that is just the light forgetting how to bend around the table. *Did you turn off the stove?* The kettle has been boiling since July; it hums your name in a low, rusted register, a frequency meant only for moths. A teacup on the counter holds four years of dry rain. I try to pull your chin from the back of my eyelids, but the silvering is scratched. A thumbprint over your left temple. A smudge of ash where your laugh used to sit.

*Speak louder. The walls are eating the sound again.*

The salt cellar tipped over. A white stain spilling across the ocean of the kitchen floor. I walk through it barefoot, leaving tracks of cold silver. *Is that you behind the wardrobe?* No, only your dark coat hanging empty, heavy with the scent of cedar, damp wool, and stale tobacco. It remembers the shape of your shoulders better than my arms do. The coat has a heart made of brass buttons. It ticks once. Twice. *Wait.* Memory is a house where the doors were painted shut while we were still inside. I claw at the wallpaper—underneath, only a field of rusted wire.

*What was the last thing you said?*

"Don’t forget the bread." Or was it about the tide? The swallows outside are flying backward today, untying their flight paths from a violet sky. I press a pewter spoon to my ear to listen for the room we used to inhabit, but it only plays the static of a dead television left on in an empty house. *I am trying to find the corner where we met.* It slid beneath the floorboards. It sank into the cellar alongside the preserves and the stopped clocks. I reach into the floor. My fingers come back dripping with dark, cold syrup. 

*Are you cold?* 

Your name is a smooth stone under my tongue. If I swallow it, I will sink. If I spit it out, the roof will finally give way to the snow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a short piece of abstract flash fiction that feels like a stream-of-consciousness journal entry. Focus on a narrator reflecting on a dead or absent figure, using vivid, strange imagery like sweetgrass in plastic and wind through fistulae.
counterfactuals.output:
*October 14th? No. The month of salt.* 

I wrapped the alarm clock in lard-soaked linen so the ticking wouldn’t curdle the milk, but the second hand still twitches against the grease. You left the small things. A tooth. Three copper buttons. The braided sweetgrass sealed in plastic—polyethylene vacuum-packed, sweating tiny amber beads of resin against the seam. A whole meadow holding its breath forever inside a dark drawer. I press my thumb against the slick skin of the bag until it squeaks. It smells like clean, suffocated summer. You were always so terrified of decay that you choked the garden before it could drop its leaves.

Where did you put your collarbones when you walked out? Not in the soil. The soil is too loud for you. 

I woke up at three and the house was leaning south, or maybe my ribs were. Listen. It’s the low, dry draft coming off the marsh, forcing its way through the floorboards, through the bedposts, through me. The wind through fistulae—that high, unnatural whistling through channels that shouldn't exist, narrow tunnels grief bores into soft tissue. A flute carved out of scar tissue and old bypasses. *Hiss. Whistle. Hold.* It plays the exact pitch of your voice when you told me the sky was just a bruised lung.

I ate a handful of frost this morning because I thought it was your hair. 

The tap drips in binary. 0100. You are the zero. I am the remnant voltage humming in the copper after the power station burns down. In the hall closet, your wool coat still holds the hollow curve of your shoulder blades, but when I reach into the sleeve, it’s only dry lint and bone-meal. I write your name on the kitchen glass, but the sun bakes it into salt. 

The grass stays green in its bag. It doesn't rot. It doesn't breathe. It will outlive the house, outlive the whistle in my side, still green and trapped and dry as bone when the wind finally blows the roof away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a poem-in-prose about waking up heavy from a strange dream, arguing with a ghost, and the failure of language to offer comfort? Keep the style choppy and avant-garde.
counterfactuals.output:
Gravity: a bucket of soaked lime. I wake up backwards. The dream is still pinned to the optic nerve—a long corridor made of boiling tin, a dog that spoke in your cadence. The mattress sags under five hundred pounds of sleep-sediment. Blood like cold porridge. 

You are at the foot of the bed. Not a shadow, exactly. A tear in the wallpaper. A density where the light refuses to fold. 

We begin the quarrel. It is an ancient, rusted mechanism. 

*You:* The floor is missing. 
*Me:* The floor is pine. 
*You:* It rots under your heels. Look down. 

I don't look down. I throw a word at your sternum—*Departure*—but it drops short, heavy, a dead sparrow on the rug. Syntax breaks at the joint. I try to construct a clause that acts as a wall, a shield, a blunt refusal, but the grammar collapses into wet lint. 

You answer in cold steam. You say: *Remember the salt.* 
I scream: *That wasn't me, that was the house.* 

The argument is all shins and elbows. No traction. I reach into my throat for something soft, a syllable of solace, a warm blanket of a noun—*Mercy*, or *Enough*, or *Morning*—and my mouth fills with metal filings. The alphabet is an empty cabinet. The dictionary: a box of dead bees. 

Language offers no wool here. It is just dry throat-noise, clicking teeth, signifiers sliding off the edge of the nightstand. *Comfort* sags like wet cardboard. *Peace* is a mistranslation of a void. 

You lean forward. You have no breath, yet you blow the candle out. 

The room stays leaden. The light comes in sideways, sharp as a rusted nail, and the sentence I was building to save myself dissolves into pure, untranslatable static.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short creative text starting with waking up from a dream, incorporating themes of unperformed daily rituals, stolen moments, and a father's ashes.
counterfactuals.output:
The sound of his voice—booming and absurdly cheerful—was still ringing in my ears when the dream collapsed back into the dim, cool reality of the bedroom. For a heartbeat, I stayed frozen, listening for his heavy footsteps down the hall, forgetting that gravity had ceased to apply to him six weeks ago.

I lay still, watching the dust motes suspended in the pale slit of light between the curtains. The day demanded its usual choreography, but I let the cues pass. The kettle remained cold on the stove. The morning stretch went unextended, the blinds unpulled, the newspaper left damp on the front step. My carefully constructed rituals, built over years to keep the chaos at bay, sat abandoned in the quiet house like unwashed dishes.

I slipped out from beneath the duvet to claim the only thing that felt real: these stolen moments in the blue hush before the sun rose, before the sympathy texts began, before I had to put on a face for the world.

Barefoot, I walked into the living room and sat on the floor beside the small wooden box on the lower shelf. It was smaller than he had been, impossibly light for a man who used to fill every room with his booming presence. I pressed my forehead against the smooth mahogany, feeling the cold stillness of his ashes within. He had always been a man of action, always moving, yet here we were together in the quiet—both of us paused, both of us waiting for a morning that felt real enough to start.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a brief, fragmented prose piece exploring the emotional clarity that comes with accepting someone's absence, using surreal sensory details and broken syntax.
counterfactuals.output:
The air, peeled back. Tastes of tin and frozen mint.

Your name—a dried cicada on the windowsill. I swept it. Watched it turn to grey flour in the sun. No crunch.

The phantom limb, unhitched at last. The socket left behind is smooth as milk glass. Cold to the palm, but steady. Sunlight enters the kitchen sideways now, heavy with the scent of wet copper. It cuts the floor into three sharp triangles. You are in none of them.

Not behind the breath. Not under the tongue.

A sudden, crystalline tilt. The silence no longer hums your pulse; it has edges now. Blue-rimmed. Solid. I press my shoulder against the empty space where you used to lean—it does not yield. It holds me up.

The chair is only oak. The latch, only iron. 

Zero. Such a bright, hollow math. 

I inhale silver wire. Exhale the entire year.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
